case_name: A. Ramaswamy Dikshitulu and Others v Government of A. P. and Others
facts: The State of Andhra Pradesh enacted the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987 providing for abolition of all rights whether hereditary, contractual or otherwise of any person who is an Archaka or a Mirasidar or a Mathadhipati or any other office holder of office in any religious institution.
Some of the writ petitions filed before the High Court was transferred to this Court. On 19.3.1996 this Court disposed of these matters by upholding the validity of the Act.

The basic point raised in these review petitions is that this Court has in several decisions explained the scope of the said provisions and it has been held therein that religious practices or performances of acts in pursuance of the religious belief are as much a part of religion as faith or belief in a particular doctrine;

that what constitutes an essential part of a religion has to be decided by the court with reference to the doctrine of a particular religion and includes practices which are regarded by the community as a part of its religion;
That the protection is only permissible where the practices is a religious one or the affairs are affairs in matters of religion;
The contentions raised by the petitioners are based on the decisions of this Court in Commissioner, HRE v. L.T. Swamiar, AIR 1954 SC 282 and Venkatramana Devaru v. State of Mysore, AIR 1958 SC 255

It is also urged that some of the observations in the judgment under review are self contradictory and that the whole approach is influenced by the basic assumption that religion should be equated to 'Dharma',
issues: What constitutes an essential part of a religion?
What practices are protected under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution?
How to determine whether a particular practice is a matter of religion?
What is the scope of religious freedom and practices expanded in previous cases?
petitioner_arguments: The decision sought to be reviewed goes counter to the principles of religious freedom and practices expanded in the said cases.
Some of the observations in the judgment under review are self contradictory and that the whole approach is influenced by the basic assumption that religion should be equated to 'Dharma',
court_reasoning: This Court has been cautious to observe that certain practices will be treated as part of religion only if they are regarded by the said religion as its essential and integral part and otherwise, even purely secular practices which are not essential or integral to the religion will be clothed a religious form to claim protection under these provisions.
The task of disengaging the secular from the religious may not be easy but it must nevertheless be attempted in dealing with claims of protection under Articles 25 and 26
